Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: This widespread species ranges from central Algeria, central and southern Tunisia to western Libya (Wilms and Böhme 2001, Wagner et al. 2011, Bauer et al. 2017). The eastern extent of its range is not clear, and records from northeastern Libya and Egypt are thought to be in error, and those from Cyreniaca are considered doubtful (Bauer et al. 2017 and refs therein). Bauer et al. (2017) nonetheless map a cluster of three records in northeastern Libya, possibly disjunctly from the main range.
documentation.population: This species is locally common and abundant in parts of its range in Morocco and Algeria, but it is rare in Tunisia. While it remains one of the least-studied lizards in North Africa across its range it is thought likely to be at risk of serious decline (Kechnebbou et al. 2019). Poaching is heavy in Tunisia, where it is the only member of the genus, and it may have declined recently in this country as a result of this exploitation (Kechnebbou et al. 2019). These authors recorded densities of 1-83 burrows / km2 as a result of intensive targeted searches; by contrast related species in Algeria, Egypt and Arabia can reach densities of up to 200-630 / km2. It is unknown whether this reflects regional variation, natural rarity or the result of population declines driven by some combination of exploitation and habitat loss (Kechnebbou et al. 2019).
documentation.habitats: It is found in arid areas with rocky slopes in mountain valleys with oueds and dense vegetation. It can be found in palm oases and fields. This species lives in burrows; Kechnebbou et al. (2019) found that, at their study site in Tunisia's Matmata Mountains, active burrows formed clusters of 1-5 burrows and were preferentially (88% of 106) dug on slopes with loose rock and sparse vegetation. Burrows in this region were generally found in areas of mixed sandy and rocky substrate, and sometimes in open sand, but never in areas with thick layers of stones (Kechnebbou et al. 2019). The uneven distribution of burrows in this study may indicate environmental or biological requirements that have not yet been identified, but may be associated with a requirement for soils with good drainage (Kechnebbou et al. 2019). The female lays two clutches averaging 23 eggs. The diet consists mainly of plant material, with a preference for fresh vegetation that may assist water uptake in an arid region observed by Kechnebbou et al. 2019). All age classes include insects in their diet, although adults may be almost strictly herbivorous (Kechnebbou et al. 2019 and refs therein).
documentation.threats: This species might be threatened by overharvesting for the international pet trade, and by domestic use for food and medicinal purposes. Additionally, many animals are killed on roads. Kechnebbou et al. (2019) observed impacts from grazing or from collection of stones for building material (which is likely to degrade the species' habitat due to its preference for burrow sites with some stone cover, at least in this area) at nearly 50% of their 25 sample sites.
documentation.measures: This species is listed in Appendix II of CITES. It is also found in protected areas in parts of its range.
documentation.use_trade: This species is commonly eaten across its range and is exploited for traditional medicine in Tunisia - where it is believed to be an effective remedy for a very wide range of illnesses - and likely elsewhere (Kechnebbou et al. 2019). Live animals are captured and kept in homes as a traditional ward against witchcraft (Kechnebbou et al. 2019). Both live animals and skins are exploited for the tourist trade (Kechnebbou et al. 2019), and there is some international trade as a pet.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Near Threatened because this species is thought to be in significant decline as a result of heavy exploitation, principally for food and traditional medicine, and while it is at least locally common it occurs at comparatively low densities in the one area from which recent data exist, but baseline data is not sufficient to conclude that this decline has exceeded 30% over three generations and the species' generation length is unclear. It is consequently close to qualifying for Vulnerable applying Criterion A.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Wilms et al. (2009) recognized Uromastyx nigriventris from Morocco and western Algeria, previously treated as a subspecies of U. acanthinura, as a distinct species on the basis of genetic evidence.
